traps.trap: Most common gallstone type is cholesterol, not mixed as the PYQ key expects

probes.stem_idea: As per the usual PYQ key, which is the most common type of gallstone?
probes.correct: Mixed stones
probes.note: the trap is the modern-text answer; pigment options are plausible fillers for learners who think of Indian haemolysis burden

probes.stem_idea: A stem lists mixed, cholesterol, black and brown stones. Which approach gets the key while keeping the truth?
probes.correct: Pick mixed for the key, knowing cholesterol and mixed together form most stones
distractor_set: Pick cholesterol, because Western texts call it the commonest
Pick black pigment, because haemolysis is common in India
Pick brown pigment, because infection is common in India

traps.diagnoses: Learner prefers the modern textbook answer and does not know that the exam key follows an older, grouped convention.
traps.first_wrong_step: Treats 'most common' as a single fact instead of asking which source the question follows.

repair.strategy: E5: teach both, 'PYQs expected mixed; texts group cholesterol and mixed as the majority'

traps.retest: contrast-form stem later in the exam-traps segment
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you know both the key and the text. Recovered: you now hold both versions. Open: remember the exam key is mixed, and that cholesterol plus mixed is the majority.

traps.trap: Ultrasound is the answer to 'most sensitive and specific' for acute cholecystitis; CT as initial test

probes.stem_idea: Most sensitive and specific test for acute cholecystitis?
probes.correct: HIDA scan
probes.note: ultrasound is the first-test habit carried into a confirmatory stem

probes.stem_idea: Fever and RUQ pain with positive Murphy's sign in an outpatient; what is the first imaging test?
probes.correct: Ultrasonography
probes.note: tests the reverse error: over-correcting to HIDA for 'first'

probes.stem_idea: Ultrasound is equivocal in a septic post-operative patient; which finding on which test confirms cystic duct obstruction?
probes.correct: Non-filling of the gallbladder on HIDA with tracer in the duodenum
distractor_set: Wall thickening and pericholecystic fluid on repeat CT
Dilated duct with stone on MRCP
Gas in the wall on plain X-ray

traps.diagnoses: Learner has one rung on the investigation ladder (ultrasound) and does not separate first-line from confirmatory.
traps.first_wrong_step: Reads 'investigation of choice' as 'first investigation' and never checks for 'most sensitive / specific / gold standard'.

repair.strategy: E8: ladder of tests with what each answers (US first, HIDA confirms, CT for complications, MRCP for duct)

traps.retest: vignette (first test) and mechanism (confirmation) after the ladder is built
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you read the wording of the question. Recovered: you now split first-line from confirmatory. Open: you answer 'ultrasound' to every gallbladder test; read for first versus most accurate.

traps.trap: Ultrasound, CT or diagnostic ERCP chosen for CBD stones instead of MRCP

probes.stem_idea: Non-invasive investigation of choice for common bile duct stones?
probes.correct: MRCP
probes.note: ERCP is wrong on the word non-invasive; the wrong model is 'the duct test I know is ERCP'

probes.stem_idea: Jaundiced patient with gallstones on ultrasound; you want to confirm a duct stone without a procedure. Next step?
probes.correct: MRCP

traps.diagnoses: Learner assumes the test that finds gallbladder stones also finds duct stones, or treats ERCP as a purely diagnostic test.
traps.first_wrong_step: Does not separate gallbladder imaging from duct imaging, and ignores that ERCP carries the therapeutic role.

repair.strategy: E8: extend the ladder to the duct: MRCP non-invasive, EUS for small stones, ERCP diagnose and treat

traps.retest: vignette form after the TR2 ladder
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you place MRCP, EUS and ERCP correctly. Recovered: you now keep ERCP for treatment. Open: you use gallbladder tests for duct stones.

traps.trap: Biliary colic is truly colicky, so day-long pain with fever is still biliary colic

probes.stem_idea: Which best describes the pain of biliary colic?
probes.correct: Steady pain that settles within a few hours
distractor_set: Intermittent waves of pain every few minutes
Persistent pain for over 6 hours with fever
Pain only after meals, never radiating

probes.stem_idea: Obese woman with RUQ pain for 24 hours, fever, tender RUQ, positive Murphy's sign. Diagnosis?
probes.correct: Acute cholecystitis

probes.stem_idea: What separates biliary colic from acute cholecystitis at the gallbladder?
probes.correct: Transient stone obstruction without inflammation of the wall
distractor_set: Smooth muscle spasm against a stone in waves
Stone permanently impacted in the CBD

traps.diagnoses: Learner takes the name 'colic' as the character of the pain and has no duration-and-inflammation boundary between colic and cholecystitis.
traps.first_wrong_step: Lets the word 'colic' define the pain instead of the time course and the presence of wall inflammation.

repair.strategy: E1: contrasting cases, colic (steady, under 6 h, no fever) beside cholecystitis (persistent, fever, tender, Murphy)

traps.retest: vignette and mechanism after the contrast
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you used duration and fever, not the name. Recovered: you now separate the two. Open: you still call persistent painful RUQ disease colic.

traps.trap: Courvoisier's law applies to any palpable gallbladder, so it always means malignancy

probes.stem_idea: Fever, tender RUQ mass, no jaundice; what does Courvoisier's law say?
probes.correct: It does not apply, as it concerns a jaundiced patient, and empyema or mucocele fits
distractor_set: Malignant obstruction of the distal bile duct

probes.stem_idea: Which statement is Courvoisier's law?
probes.correct: In a jaundiced patient, a palpable non-tender gallbladder is unlikely to be due to stones
distractor_set: A palpable gallbladder excludes gallstone disease
A tender palpable gallbladder with fever suggests carcinoma

traps.diagnoses: Learner holds the law as a one-line rule about the gallbladder and drops the jaundice and non-tender qualifiers.
traps.first_wrong_step: Drops 'in a jaundiced patient' and applies the rule to every palpable gallbladder.

repair.strategy: E7: highlight the qualifier; contrast jaundice plus non-tender with tender mass and no jaundice

traps.retest: recognition form after the vignette
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you kept the jaundice qualifier. Recovered: you now check jaundice first. Open: you read the sign as 'palpable means cancer'.

traps.trap: TG18 suspected versus definite diagnosis set built wrongly (A+B vs A+B+C)

probes.stem_idea: By TG18, a suspected diagnosis of acute cholecystitis needs which combination?
probes.correct: One local sign plus one systemic sign
distractor_set: One local sign, one systemic sign and imaging findings
Ultrasound stones plus one local sign

probes.stem_idea: Patient has Murphy's sign and fever; imaging is not yet done. At what TG18 level is the diagnosis?
probes.correct: Suspected
distractor_set: Not diagnosable until imaging is done
Not yet suspected, needs a second local sign

traps.diagnoses: Learner reads TG18 as one pool of signs rather than a three-part rule where imaging upgrades suspected to definite.
traps.first_wrong_step: Does not build the rule as A plus B for suspected, then add C for definite.

repair.strategy: E2: rebuild the set from its logic (A local, B systemic, C imaging) and retest with a level question

traps.retest: vignette giving signs without imaging
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you built suspected and definite from A, B and C. Recovered: the rule is now a sequence. Open: you mix the levels; rebuild A+B and A+B+C.

traps.trap: TG18 grading numbers swapped with familiar sepsis or lab cut-offs

probes.stem_idea: Which finding makes TG18 Grade II (moderate) acute cholecystitis?
probes.correct: WBC above 18,000/mm3

probes.stem_idea: A single organ dysfunction criterion qualifying as Grade III?
probes.correct: Serum creatinine above 2.0 mg/dL
probes.note: stem wording 'any one' also quietly teaches that Grade III needs one system only

traps.diagnoses: Learner substitutes everyday cut-offs from sepsis and routine labs for TG18-specific figures.
traps.first_wrong_step: Recalls a familiar threshold for the lab instead of the one tied to this grading system.

repair.strategy: E6: anchor numbers to meaning (severe means clearly abnormal, so the cut-offs are higher than screening values); retest in another form

traps.retest: grade-II and grade-III numbers swapped between the two probes
traps.report_hint: Avoided: your numbers are TG18-specific. Recovered: the cut-offs now stick. Open: you use screening cut-offs; review the TG18 card.

traps.trap: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the answer in every TG18 grade

probes.stem_idea: Elderly man with acute cholecystitis, hypotension on noradrenaline and raised creatinine. First management?
probes.correct: Organ support and gallbladder drainage
distractor_set: Conservative care, interval cholecystectomy at 6-8 weeks

probes.stem_idea: Grade II acute cholecystitis in a patient unfit for surgery; what is the plan?
probes.correct: Initial medical treatment or gallbladder drainage, with surgery deferred
distractor_set: Cholecystectomy at once in the index admission
Cholecystectomy only after 6-8 weeks in every patient

probes.stem_idea: Why does Grade III change the order of treatment?
probes.correct: Organ dysfunction makes surgery unsafe until the patient is supported and the gallbladder drained
distractor_set: Grade III disease never needs surgery
The 72 hour window has already closed
Drainage cures the disease and makes surgery redundant

traps.diagnoses: Learner holds one answer for acute cholecystitis and does not add the grade and fitness step.
traps.first_wrong_step: Skips 'how sick and how fit is this patient' and goes straight to the operation.

traps.retest: sequence form with a different grade after the vignette
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you graded before choosing. Recovered: grade now sets your first step. Open: you operate first in every grade; grade III drains first.

traps.trap: Interval cholecystectomy at 6-8 weeks (older key) chosen over early surgery

probes.stem_idea: Current treatment of choice for acute calculous cholecystitis in a fit patient?
probes.correct: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy in the index admission
distractor_set: Conservative treatment, then interval cholecystectomy at 6-8 weeks
Antibiotics alone, surgery only if symptoms recur

probes.stem_idea: Fit patient, 48 hours of symptoms, mild disease, admitted. Plan?
probes.correct: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy during this admission
distractor_set: Discharge on antibiotics and operate after 6-8 weeks
Wait for the pain to settle before booking surgery

traps.diagnoses: Learner studied from older books and keeps the 'cool it down first' plan as the answer.
traps.first_wrong_step: Believes inflamed tissue must settle before operating, so delay seems safer.

traps.retest: vignette later, then again within the TG18 management items
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you used current practice. Recovered: you moved from the old key. Open: you still choose interval surgery; know the old key and the current answer.

traps.trap: Asymptomatic gallstones should be removed because stones are a risk

probes.stem_idea: 2 cm stones found incidentally on ultrasound for fatty liver, no symptoms ever. Best management?
probes.correct: Expectant management, no surgery

probes.stem_idea: Which asymptomatic patient merits prophylactic cholecystectomy?
probes.correct: A patient with a porcelain gallbladder
distractor_set: A 30-year-old woman with a 2 cm stone
An obese patient with multiple small stones
A pregnant woman with incidental stones

probes.stem_idea: Approximate yearly risk that an asymptomatic stone starts causing symptoms?
probes.correct: 1-2% per year

traps.diagnoses: Learner stretches 'stones cause cholecystitis and cancer' to every stone and ignores how low the yearly risk is.
traps.first_wrong_step: Treats the presence of a stone as the indication, rather than symptoms or a specific high-risk feature.

traps.retest: contrast form of 'who gets prophylactic surgery' and the numbers probe
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you know most stones are left alone. Recovered: you now name the exceptions. Open: you operate on all stones; indications are symptoms or specific risks.

traps.trap: Ursodeoxycholic acid dissolves any stone

probes.stem_idea: In which patient is ursodeoxycholic acid likely to dissolve stones?
probes.correct: Small radiolucent cholesterol stones with a functioning gallbladder
distractor_set: Stones in an acutely inflamed gallbladder with fever

probes.stem_idea: Hereditary spherocytosis, small multiple stones with symptoms. Is dissolution therapy sensible?
probes.correct: No, because pigment stones do not dissolve; treat by cholecystectomy
distractor_set: Yes, a 6-12 month course of ursodeoxycholic acid as the stones are small
Yes, ursodeoxycholic acid plus cholecystectomy later

traps.diagnoses: Learner remembers 'UDCA dissolves gallstones' and drops the stone-type, size and gallbladder-function qualifiers.
traps.first_wrong_step: Takes the drug-of-choice line without its conditions.

traps.retest: vignette using a pigment stone surface
traps.report_hint: Avoided: you checked who the drug suits. Recovered: you now apply the qualifiers. Open: you give UDCA to any stone.

traps.trap: Black and brown pigment stone associations swapped

probes.stem_idea: Which stone is linked to chronic haemolysis and cirrhosis?
probes.correct: Black pigment stones

probes.stem_idea: Soft, earthy stones in the bile ducts of a patient with Ascaris and recurrent cholangitis. Stone type and site?
probes.correct: Brown pigment stones, formed in the bile ducts
distractor_set: Black pigment stones, formed in the gallbladder
Black pigment stones, formed in the bile ducts
Cholesterol stones, formed in the bile ducts

traps.diagnoses: Learner files both pigment stones as one type and cannot link cause and site to colour.

traps.report_hint: Avoided: black and brown are separate in your head. Recovered: you now pair colour with cause and site. Open: swap risk; black is haemolysis, brown is infection.

traps.trap: Bouveret's syndrome and gallstone ileus swapped as to site

probes.stem_idea: Gastric outlet obstruction from a gallstone impacted in the duodenum is called?
probes.correct: Bouveret's syndrome

probes.stem_idea: Elderly woman with small-bowel obstruction, pneumobilia and an ectopic stone. Diagnosis and usual site?
probes.correct: Gallstone ileus, impacted in the terminal ileum
distractor_set: Bouveret's syndrome, impacted in the duodenum
Gallstone ileus, impacted at the pylorus
Mirizzi syndrome, with a cholecystocholedochal fistula

traps.diagnoses: Learner knows both are stone obstructions and treats the eponym and site as interchangeable.
traps.first_wrong_step: Does not anchor the eponym to the site of obstruction (outlet versus terminal ileum).

traps.trap: Charcot's triad and Reynolds' pentad blurred

probes.stem_idea: Which is Charcot's triad in acute cholangitis?
probes.correct: Fever with rigors, jaundice, RUQ pain
distractor_set: Fever, jaundice, RUQ pain, hypotension and confusion

probes.correct: Reynolds' pentad

traps.retest: vignette naming the set

traps.trap: Emphysematous cholecystitis is caused by E. coli, as in any infected gallbladder

probes.stem_idea: Most common organism in emphysematous cholecystitis?
probes.correct: Clostridium perfringens

probes.stem_idea: Gas in the gallbladder wall on plain X-ray. Which patient and organism fit?

distractor_set: Middle-aged woman on oral contraceptives, Klebsiella

traps.diagnoses: Learner carries the commonest organism in infected bile to the gas-forming variant and imagines the usual gallstone patient.

traps.trap: Seeing two structures is enough for the critical view of safety

probes.stem_idea: Besides two structures entering the gallbladder, what completes the critical view of safety?
probes.correct: Triangle cleared of fat and the lower third of the gallbladder separated from the cystic plate
distractor_set: Nothing more, two and only two structures is the whole view

Divide the first tubular structure seen, then confirm

traps.trap: Commonest cause of major bile duct injury is vascular or bleeding

probes.stem_idea: Commonest cause of major bile duct injury in cholecystectomy?

traps.trap: Mirizzi syndrome is a stone in the CBD rather than external compression

probes.stem_idea: What causes the jaundice in Mirizzi syndrome?
probes.correct: A stone in Hartmann's pouch or cystic duct compressing the common hepatic duct
distractor_set: A stone passed into the common bile duct blocking its lumen
A stone impacted at the ampulla
Ascending infection of an obstructed duct

probes.stem_idea: Jaundice with an impacted stone in the cystic duct and extrinsic narrowing of the common hepatic duct on imaging. Diagnosis?

traps.trap: Acalculous cholecystitis is milder than calculous because no stone obstructs

probes.stem_idea: Compared with calculous cholecystitis, acalculous cholecystitis?
probes.correct: Has more gangrene and perforation and higher mortality
distractor_set: Runs a milder course as there is no stone to obstruct

Behaves the same as calculous disease

traps.retest: vignette in an ICU setting

distractor_set: Conservative care, interval cholecystectomy at 6-8 weeks

dropped.reason: medium yield; Murphy's sign is taught in TR4 and TR7 content (K5, K55) and can be a one-line aside without its own branch
medium yield; near-duplicate of TR8 (Grade III), and the 'any one system' rule is carried in the stem of the TR8 probe
medium yield; refuted only by an unverified exam note (K117, K70), and overlaps TR12 (prophylactic surgery); may be shown as a ⚠ aside
medium yield; Calot's upper border (K120) is a narrow PYQ-reading conflict, lowest yield after cap to 20

probe_plan: Backbone traps, met in this order: TR4 (colic vs cholecystitis, defines the disease and the red-flag course), TR2 then TR3 (the investigation ladder, gallbladder first and duct second), TR7 then TR8 (TG18 diagnosis, then grade numbers), TR11 then TR10 then TR24 (treatment: early surgery replaces interval surgery, then grade and fitness change the sequence, then the acalculous ICU case). TR23 and TR24 and TR14 and TR12 share the 'qualifier' theme and are best placed in the management and exam-trap segments. TR1 (PYQ key) can open the exam-traps segment as a low-risk warm-up for the E5 teach-both repair, which TR11 reuses later. Complication traps TR15, TR16, TR17, TR18, TR22 are association pairs and co-trap in pairs (TR16 with TR22, TR15 with TR14); TR19 with TR20 are the safe-surgery pair with TR19 as the prerequisite. TR3 and TR2 share the MRCP option so the ladder is tested as one stem family. Every trap has probes in two different forms; TR2, TR4, TR10 and TR12 get a third probe since they are the most reused. Each re-test sits at least one segment after the first surfacing, and TR24 is placed in the last segment as the cold probe. Distractors marked partial are correct-adjacent or neutral fillers, and no option serves two traps.
